# The Artificial-Language Grid {#sec-appendix-grid}

Table \ref{tbl-grid} lists every factor crossed in Experiment 1 and its levels. The three effect weights and the context weight define the language; the interaction's rank is a property of the language too, since it sets how many directions the interaction spans. Hidden width and activation belong to the learner, and the seed redraws both the language's realization and the model's initialization.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-grid
#| tbl-cap: "The Experiment 1 grid. The first five rows define an artificial language, the next two the learner, and the last is replication. Item and class ranks are held fixed so that the interaction's rank is the only one that varies. Crossing every level gives 38,400 cells; the three languages in which all three effect weights are zero contain no item-by-class structure at all and are excluded, leaving the reported total."
.k <- toy$key |> strsplit("_") |> do.call(what = rbind) |>
  as.data.frame() |> lapply(\(x) sort(unique(as.numeric(x))))
lv <- function(x) paste(formatC(x, format = "g"), collapse = ", ")
tibble::tribble(
  ~factor,              ~levels,
  "item weight",        lv(.k[[1]]),
  "class weight",       lv(.k[[2]]),
  "interaction weight", lv(.k[[3]]),
  "context weight",     lv(.k[[4]]),
  "interaction rank",   lv(sort(unique(toy$r_int))),
  "hidden width",       lv(sort(unique(toy$d))),
  "activation",         "linear, ReLU",
  "seed",               lv(sort(unique(toy$seed)))) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "ll", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("factor", "levels")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  pack_rows("language", 1, 5) |>
  pack_rows("learner", 6, 7) |>
  pack_rows("replication", 8, 8)
```

Item rank is fixed at `r unique(toy$r_item)` and class rank at `r unique(toy$r_class)`, so the structure a language requires is `r unique(toy$r_item) + unique(toy$r_class)` directions plus the interaction's rank, running from `r min(toy$rank)` to `r max(toy$rank)`. Against the widths above, a language needs between `r g(min(toy$capacity), 3)` and `r g(max(toy$capacity), 1)` times as many dimensions as the layer has. Of the `r cm(nrow(toy))` runs, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(toy$converged))` trained to convergence.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Validating the Measure {#sec-appendix-validate}

Experiment 1 builds structure into a language and measures a trained model's representation. However, that approach cannot distinguish a failure of the measure from the model representing the language differently than the structure it was given. Here we remove that ambiguity by constructing representations in which $\mu$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are set directly, with no model or training, and passing the result through the same analysis used for the language models. Ground truth therefore exists at the level where the measure operates.

```{r}
#| label: setup-validate
#| include: false
val <- rd("validate_measure.csv")
v_rec <- val |> filter(n_obs == 24, d >= 768) |> group_by(planted_int) |>
  summarize(n = n(), measured = median(size_interaction),
            lo = quantile(size_interaction, .025), hi = quantile(size_interaction, .975),
            flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop")
v_null <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", med = median(size_interaction),
              p95 = quantile(size_interaction, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "class effect", med = median(size_class),
              p95 = quantile(size_class, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0) |> group_by(n_obs) |>
    summarize(effect = "item effect", med = median(size_item),
              p95 = quantile(size_item, .95),
              flagged = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
# False-positive rate of the re-split test BY WIDTH: how often a truly-zero effect's interval
# excludes zero. This is what says whether a small measured effect at a given width is a real
# detection or the test's own floor, and it tells the reader where the test is calibrated.
v_fp_d <- bind_rows(
  val |> filter(planted_int == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "interaction", fp = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_class == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "class", fp = mean(size_class_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"),
  val |> filter(planted_item == 0, n_obs == 24) |> group_by(d) |>
    summarize(effect = "item", fp = mean(size_item_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop"))
fpget <- function(eff, dd) v_fp_d$fp[v_fp_d$effect == eff & v_fp_d$d == dd]
v_ov <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap == 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d), .groups = "drop")
# The power side: a KNOWN fraction of the class direction placed inside the item subspace. The
# measured overlap should rise above chance and be flagged outside its own random-orientation null.
v_ov_power <- val |> filter(!is.na(leak_item_into_class), n_obs == 24, planted_overlap > 0) |>
  group_by(d) |> summarize(measured = median(leak_item_into_class),
                           lo = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .025),
                           hi = quantile(leak_item_into_class, .975),
                           chance = median(k_class / d),
                           detected = mean(leak_item_into_class_outside %in% c(TRUE, "TRUE")),
                           .groups = "drop")
vget <- function(eff, obs, col) v_null[[col]][v_null$effect == eff & v_null$n_obs == obs]
```

Specifically, we generated representations with known values of $\mu$, $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$, varying the number of items, classes, representation dimensions, observations per pairing, and noise level across the range used in the experiments. Components were centered to satisfy their defining constraints and rescaled to predetermined shares of the total squared length. The grid included the same factorial Experiment 1 runs, mapped into share space, the three compositions measured in Experiment 2, item counts from 27 to 180, two and four classes, widths from 8 to 2048, 10, 24, and 100 observations per item and class, three noise levels, and five seeds. We also generated orthogonal and known non-orthogonal item and class effects: the orthogonal condition draws $\alpha$ and $\beta$ independently, while the non-orthogonal condition places a known fraction of $\beta$ along $\alpha$'s leading singular direction. In total, this gave `r cm(nrow(val))` runs.

At 24 observations per item and class, the measured interaction matches the one it was given across the whole range (Table \ref{tbl-val-recovery}), and is flagged in essentially every run where anything was present and about one in twenty where nothing was.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-recovery
#| tbl-cap: "Recovery at 24 observations per item and class in 768 or more dimensions, pooled over noise levels, item counts, and widths. Brackets are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles across runs."
v_rec |>
  transmute(`specified` = g(planted_int, 3),
            runs = n,
            `measured` = sprintf("%.4f [%.4f, %.4f]", measured, lo, hi),
            `flagged` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * flagged)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

All three effects read essentially zero when a component is set to zero, at every sample size, and each is flagged at approximately the nominal 5% rate (Table \ref{tbl-val-null}).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-null
#| tbl-cap: "What the measure reports when an effect is set to exactly zero, by observations per item and class, pooled over every other axis of the validation grid."
v_null |>
  transmute(effect, observations = n_obs,
            median = g(med, 5), `95th pct` = g(p95, 4),
            flagged = ifelse(is.na(flagged), "---", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * flagged))) |>
  arrange(effect, observations) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

The false-positive rate varies somewhat with representation width and component, particularly at small widths, but remains below 10% throughout the validation grid except for the class effect at the narrowest width, where it reaches 14% (Table \ref{tbl-val-fpd}). The language-model analyses use $d\geq768$, where the rates are closer to the nominal level.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-fpd
#| tbl-cap: "How often a component set to exactly zero is flagged, by width and by effect."
v_fp_d |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = effect, values_from = fp) |>
  transmute(`width d` = d,
            item = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * item),
            class = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * class),
            interaction = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * interaction)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-overlap
#| tbl-cap: "Measured item-class overlap when the two effects are constructed orthogonal, at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median over the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets. The *chance* column is the analytic level of Appendix \\ref{sec-appendix-math}."
v_ov |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 5),
            `analytic chance` = g(chance, 5)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

With orthogonal item and class effects, the measured overlap tracks the chance level across representation widths (Table \ref{tbl-val-overlap}). When a known fraction of the class direction is placed inside the item subspace, the measured overlap rises above chance and is detected in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v_ov_power$detected[v_ov_power$d == 2048])` of runs at $d=2048$ (Table \ref{tbl-val-power}). Thus, the measure recovers both the expected chance overlap under orthogonality and genuine non-orthogonality.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-power
#| tbl-cap: "Measured item-class overlap when a fraction of the class direction is placed INSIDE the item subspace (non-orthogonal), at 24 observations per item and class. *Measured* is the median over the runs at that width with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles in brackets; *chance* is the analytic random-orientation level; *detected* is the fraction of runs whose overlap falls outside that null's 95% interval."
v_ov_power |>
  transmute(`width d` = d, measured = ci(measured, lo, hi, 4), chance = g(chance, 5),
            detected = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * detected)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Within-cell spread {#sec-appendix-spread}

The interaction is a residual, and a residual absorbs whatever noise the terms before it do not. Each cell mean is an average over the contexts a word appears in, so it carries sampling error of order the within-cell spread over the number of tokens; estimated within a single split, the interaction would inherit that error and grow with the spread whether or not any interaction was present.

The cross-split product forecloses this rather than reducing it. The two estimates come from disjoint halves of a cell's tokens, so their errors are independent and mean-zero, and the expectation of their inner product is the true squared length with no variance term: the spread enters the variance of the estimate and not its expectation. This holds for any spread, and for a spread that differs from cell to cell.

Table \ref{tbl-val-noise} shows it. Holding the planted interaction fixed and scaling the within-cell spread by fifty leaves the measured value where it is, and where nothing was planted the false-positive rate stays at the nominal level rather than rising with the spread. If anything the measure drifts slightly low at the widest spread.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-val-noise
#| tbl-cap: "Recovery against within-cell spread, in 768 or more dimensions, pooled over item counts, widths and sample sizes. *Noise* is the multiple of the baseline within-cell spread the representations were generated with. *Measured* is the median across runs and *flagged* the share whose re-split interval excludes zero, which should sit at 5% in the rows where nothing was planted."
val |> filter(d >= 768, planted_int %in% c(0, 0.1, 0.2)) |>
  group_by(planted_int, noise_ratio) |>
  summarize(runs = n(), measured = median(size_interaction),
            flagged = mean(size_interaction_excludes_zero), .groups = "drop") |>
  transmute(specified = g(planted_int, 2), noise = paste0(g(noise_ratio, 0), "x"),
            runs, measured = g(measured, 4),
            flagged = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * flagged)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "rrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("specified", "noise", "runs", "measured", "flagged")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

Two things outside the validation grid point the same way. The independence the argument rests on would fail if a cell's tokens were not independent draws, the same word in the same class pulled repeatedly from one passage; across the items measured here, 2.6% of occurrences share a sentence with another occurrence of the same word in the same class, and the most affected item reaches 15%. And in Experiment 1, where the spread is manipulated directly rather than observed, raising the context weight *lowers* the measured interaction (Table \ref{tbl-lang}), which is the opposite of what an inflation account predicts.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# The Decomposition {#sec-appendix-math}

## The item-by-class means {#sec-appendix-math-grid}

![Each word in each class is observed in many contexts, and those observations are averaged within the pairing to give one of the item-by-class means. Every one of them is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and every item appears in every class.](fig-grid.pdf){#fig-grid width="100%"}

A word used in a given class is observed in many contexts, and the representation differs a little in each. Averaging those observations within the pairing gives one of the item-by-class means: for items $i \in \{1,\dots,I\}$ crossed with classes $c \in \{1,\dots,C\}$, $M[i,c] \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the mean representation of item $i$ in class $c$ (@fig-grid). An item observed in only one class is dropped, as is an item with fewer than 10 tokens in either class, so the set is complete and every mean rests on a comparable number of observations. Because every item appears at every class, the means arrange into $I$ by $C$ positions, and the rest of this appendix calls that arrangement the grid when what matters is the positions rather than the vectors sitting at them. The variation across contexts that the averaging sets aside is not discarded; it is what the two splits of @sec-measure are drawn from.

## Sizes {#sec-appendix-math-sizes}

![How many positions of the grid each component occupies. $\alpha_i$ does not depend on the class, so it occupies all $C$ positions of its row; $\beta_c$ does not depend on the item, so it occupies all $I$ positions of its column; $\gamma_{ic}$ takes its own value at every position and is never repeated.](fig-replication.pdf){#fig-replication width="100%"}

Since the effects are centered along their respective axes, their cross-terms cancel when summed over the full grid. Thus the total squared length partitions exactly:

$$
\sum_{i,c}\lVert M[i,c]-\mu\rVert^{2}
= C\sum_{i}\lVert\alpha_i\rVert^{2}
+ I\sum_{c}\lVert\beta_c\rVert^{2}
+ \sum_{i,c}\lVert\gamma_{ic}\rVert^{2},
$$

The multipliers count grid positions, since $\alpha_i$ is repeated across all $C$ classes of its row and $\beta_c$ across all $I$ items of its column while $\gamma_{ic}$ appears once (@fig-replication). Sizes are reported as shares of the total. All three terms scale linearly in $I$, so the shares do not depend on how many items there are and are comparable across categories of different size.

The above decomposition, however, ignores the role of context. In order to estimate how the three components and context vary in size, we can instead decompose each representation into its pairing mean and its deviation from that mean, giving the standard within–between partition:

$$
\sum_{x}\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^{2}
=
\underbrace{\sum_{i,c}\sum_{x\in(i,c)}
\lVert x-\hat M[i,c]\rVert^{2}}_{\text{within a pairing}}
+
\underbrace{\sum_{i,c}n_{ic}
\lVert\hat M[i,c]-\bar x\rVert^{2}}_{\text{between pairings}}.
$$

The between-pairing term is the variation partitioned into item, class, and item-by-class components above, while the within-pairing term captures variation across contexts. The resulting context variance and the $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ variance components together partition the variance of the original representations.

## The overlaps and their chance level {#sec-appendix-math-overlap}

The component sizes describe how much variation each component accounts for, but not whether the components occupy the same directions in $\mathbb{R}^d$. To measure their overlap, we project each component into a target subspace and ask how much of its squared length is retained. Specifically, we project $\alpha$ into the subspace spanned by $\beta$, $\beta$ into the subspace spanned by $\alpha$, and $\gamma$ into the subspace jointly spanned by $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $S$ is an orthonormal basis for the target subspace and $V$ is the component being projected, the overlap is

$$
\frac{\lVert VS\rVert_F^2}{\lVert V\rVert_F^2}
$$ Thus, an overlap of zero means that the component is orthogonal to the target subspace, whereas an overlap of one means that it lies entirely within it. Because the projection uses squared lengths, opposite directions contribute equally rather than canceling. We use the leading singular vectors of each target component to define its subspace, with the number of directions determined by its participation ratio. The number of directions in the target subspace therefore determines its chance overlap under random orientation.

The chance level for overlap is $r/d$, where $r$ is the dimensionality of the target subspace and $d$ is the full representation dimension. A randomly oriented component therefore has an expected fraction $r/d$ of its squared length in the target subspace. At $d=2048$, for example, the chance level is $0.0005$ for a one-dimensional class subspace. We therefore interpret observed overlaps relative to this chance level.

{{< pagebreak >}}

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Width and Orthogonality {#sec-appendix-capacity}

Whether the item and class effects are orthogonal depends on the width of the representation. @fig-toy-overlap reports that relationship from the fitted models; this appendix gives the remaining properties of the artificial-language runs.

Under ReLU, overlap stays below chance at wide layers and rises above it as the layer narrows, while the linear condition stays well below chance at every width. Varying the rank of the interaction moves that crossing only slightly, and far less than it moves the interaction's own overlap with the margins.

At low widths, the representations also vary substantially across runs, with this variability decreasing as width increases. For example, two runs of the same language differ by `r g(seedspan(8, "item"), 2)` in the item effect and `r g(seedspan(8, "class"), 2)` in the class effect at width 8, compared with `r g(seedspan(32, "item"), 2)` and `r g(seedspan(32, "class"), 2)` at width 32. This variability reflects the different ways models can distribute information when representational capacity is limited.

Two properties of the language also affect the composition of the item-by-class structure (Table \ref{tbl-lang}). Increasing the contribution of context reduces the interaction share, while increasing the item's share in the language produces a corresponding increase in its share of the representation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lang
#| tbl-cap: "How two other properties of the artificial language move the composition of the item-by-class structure, under ReLU, pooled over widths. Rows within a property partition the same runs. Values are medians of the three shares over the runs in the row."
toy_bylang |>
  transmute(property, level, runs,
            item = g(item, 3), class = g(class, 3), interaction = g(interaction, 3)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

Whether an interaction is detected at all, rather than how large it is, separates the two activations further. Every language counted here holds both an item and a class effect, so an additive one is genuinely an item part plus a class part. Across the `r cm(nullget("linear", TRUE, "n"))` of them that also contained an interaction, the linear learner's interaction interval excludes zero in `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nullget("linear", TRUE, "flagged_ez"))` of them against `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nullget("ReLU", TRUE, "flagged_ez"))` for ReLU; where the language contained no interaction the rates were `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nullget("linear", FALSE, "flagged_ez"))` and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nullget("ReLU", FALSE, "flagged_ez"))` respectively, against a test that flags a truly-zero component about 5% of the time (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-validate}). A linear learner therefore builds interaction structure it has no parameter for, and a ReLU learner registers one even where the language holds none.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Component models {#sec-appendix-component-models}

Table \ref{tbl-component-coefs} reports every coefficient of @eq-ordbeta and @fig-toy-coefs shows them.

We fit each activation separately, giving six models in all, so that the linear arm is described by the same model as the ReLU arm rather than by medians alone. We keep only runs that converged and in which at least one of the three components has a re-split interval excluding zero. That second criterion matters more here than it does for the descriptive figure: where nothing resolves, each of the three shares is a noise-sized quantity divided by a noise-sized total, so whichever component happens to land slightly positive takes nearly all of it, and the resulting value is arbitrary rather than small. Unlike the descriptive figure, we do keep languages in which a component was given no weight at all, since those runs anchor the low end of the effect-size predictors and are what identify the off-diagonal terms.

Every component and overlap model used at least `r cm(min(rdiag$n_draws))` post-warmup draws, produced no divergent transitions, and reached a bulk effective sample size of at least `r cm(round(min(rdiag$min_ess_bulk)))`. The largest $\hat{R}$ across them is `r g(max(rdiag$max_rhat), 2)`.

Because @eq-ordbeta carries a three-way interaction, the width and rank coefficients are conditional main effects: each is the effect at the mean of the other predictors rather than an effect averaged over them. The contrast in Table \ref{tbl-component-ratio} is evaluated at the same point.

@fig-toy-effects holds rank at its mean, which is the right simplification for the main text but leaves the three-way term invisible. @fig-toy-effects-full shows the same fitted surface with rank broken out as a row of facets, so the question of whether the rank an interaction requires constrains what the model represents can be read directly: were it to constrain it, the rows would differ, most visibly in the interaction column.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-component-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Every coefficient of @eq-ordbeta, in one block per measured component. *Estimate* is the posterior mean and *error* its standard deviation; the interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the posterior. The last column is the share of posterior draws above zero. Within each block the first three rows are the three effect sizes in the language and the rest are the architecture terms, where *effect size* means that block's own component."
rcoef |> filter(kind == "size") |>
  transmute(arm, component, term = label,
            estimate = g(estimate, 2), error = g(error, 2),
            ci = paste0("[", g(lo95, 2), ", ", g(hi95, 2), "]"),
            p_gt0 = g(p_gt0, 2)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("arm", "component", "term", "estimate", "error", "95% CI", "P(b > 0)")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-component-ratio
#| tbl-cap: "The sum of the width and rank coefficients, for each measured component and activation. A representation limited by how many dimensions its structure needs relative to the layer would give width and rank equal and opposite coefficients, so a sum whose interval excludes zero is evidence against that account."
rcrwd |> filter(kind == "size") |>
  transmute(arm, component, estimate = g(estimate, 2), error = g(error, 2),
            ci = paste0("[", g(lo95, 2), ", ", g(hi95, 2), "]"),
            ez = ifelse(excludes_zero, "yes", "no")) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("arm", "component", "estimate", "error", "95% CI",
                    "excludes zero")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

![Every coefficient of @eq-ordbeta, with 66% and 95% posterior intervals. Columns are the three measured components, one fitted model each. The upper block is the three effect sizes in the language, whose diagonal is the specificity check; the lower block is the architecture terms, where *effect size* refers to the panel's own component. The two blocks are drawn on separate x scales, since the language terms span a range several times wider than the architecture terms.](fig-toy-coefs.pdf){#fig-toy-coefs width="100%"}

## Overlap models {#sec-appendix-overlap-models}

Table \ref{tbl-overlap-coefs} reports every coefficient of @eq-overlap. There are four of these models, two measures crossed with the two activations, and they differ from the component models in what the architecture is crossed with: an overlap is a property of two components together, so there is no single "own" effect size to interact with width and rank, and the three effect sizes enter additively as controls instead.

The inclusion rule is the one the component models use. A run contributes if it converged and if at least one of the three components has a re-split interval excluding zero; where none does, the decomposition is noise throughout, and the directions one would project between are as arbitrary as the shares. Within that set nothing is excluded on the size of the components an overlap relates, so a component too small to orient contributes the overlap it produces, which is the value an arbitrary direction would give and is what the random-subspace baseline is there to reveal.

The outcome is the overlap divided by its own chance level and logged, so a coefficient is a multiplicative effect on that ratio and zero means no change in it. The chance level is that run's own random-subspace median, which is what makes widths comparable at all: the same raw overlap means different things at 8 dimensions and at 2048, and the median tracks the rank of the target subspace over the width closely enough that the ratio reads as a multiple of what an arbitrary direction would give.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-overlap-coefs
#| tbl-cap: "Every coefficient of @eq-overlap, in one block per measure and activation. *Estimate* is the posterior mean and *error* its standard deviation; the interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the posterior. The last column is the share of posterior draws above zero. The three effect sizes enter as additive controls, and the architecture terms are width, rank and their interaction."
rcoef |> filter(kind == "overlap") |>
  transmute(arm, measure = component, term = label,
            estimate = g(estimate, 2), error = g(error, 2),
            ci = paste0("[", g(lo95, 2), ", ", g(hi95, 2), "]"),
            p_gt0 = g(p_gt0, 2)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lllrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("arm", "measure", "term", "estimate", "error", "95% CI", "P(b > 0)")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

![The fitted surface of @eq-ordbeta with the rank of the interaction in the language broken out as rows, rather than held at its mean as in @fig-toy-effects. Columns are the three measured components and lines are hidden widths, with 95% intervals. Rows that look alike indicate that the rank an interaction requires does not constrain what the learner represents of it.](fig-toy-effects-full.pdf){#fig-toy-effects-full width="100%"}

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy-overlap
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Fitted overlap between components, as a multiple of the level an arbitrary orientation would give, against hidden width. Left: the item effect projected onto the class direction. Right: the interaction projected onto the span of both margins. The dashed line is chance; above it components share directions more than orientation alone explains, below it the learner has separated them by more than chance. Widths are drawn evenly spaced rather than to scale, since width 64 was not trained. Effect sizes are held at their means, and every run contributes: no overlap is excluded on the size of the components it relates."
#|
ARMC <- c(ReLU = UO[["gold"]], linear = UO[["green2"]])
OVLAB <- c(item_class = "item into class", int_margins = "interaction into margins",
           int_margins_int = "interaction into margins")
rpred |>
  filter(kind == "overlap", grid == "arch") |>
  mutate(arm = factor(arm, c("relu", "linear"), c("ReLU", "linear")),
         measure = factor(unname(OVLAB[component]), unname(OVLAB[c(1, 2)])),
         # Width is a designed factor with five levels and no 64, so plotting it to scale leaves
         # a double-width gap that says nothing about the result. The models fit log2(width).
         wpos = as.integer(factor(width, sort(unique(width))))) |>
  group_by(arm, measure, width, wpos) |>
  summarize(epred = median(exp(epred)), lo = median(exp(lo)), hi = median(exp(hi)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(wpos, epred, color = arm, fill = arm)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, linewidth = .35, color = UO[["grey"]]) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = .16, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .7) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = ARMC, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ARMC, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq_along(sort(unique(rpred$width))),
                     labels = sort(unique(rpred$width))) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "hidden width", y = "overlap (multiple of chance)") +
  theme_paper(9) + theme(legend.position = "top",
                         legend.margin = margin(0, 0, -6, 0),
                         panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy-effects
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-cap: "Fitted share of the representation taken by each component, against hidden width, with one line per rank of the interaction planted in the language and 95% intervals. Rows are the two activations, columns the three measured components. Effect sizes are held at their means. Were capacity the governing quantity, rank would separate the lines as strongly as width slopes them."
RNKC <- setNames(colorRampPalette(c("#F2D493", "#7A5407"))(4), sort(unique(rpred$r_int[!is.na(rpred$r_int)])))
rpred |>
  filter(kind == "size", grid == "arch") |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, c("item", "class", "interaction")),
         arm = factor(arm, c("relu", "linear"), c("ReLU", "linear"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(width, epred, color = factor(r_int), fill = factor(r_int))) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = .14, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .6) +
  facet_grid(arm ~ component,
             labeller = labeller(component = function(z) paste("measured", z))) +
  scale_color_manual(values = RNKC, name = "interaction rank\nin the language") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = RNKC, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log2", breaks = sort(unique(rpred$width))) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "hidden width", y = "share of the representation") +
  theme_paper(8) + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

# Model Details {#sec-appendix-models}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "The six models, paired by width. Training-token counts are approximate; the OPT-BabyLM models train for 20 epochs over a 100M-word corpus, which is roughly 150M tokens, so their effective token exposure is about twenty times that. *Layers* counts the transformer blocks, and the measure is applied to each block's output plus the embedding layer."
tibble::tribble(
  ~family,  ~model,          ~params, ~width, ~layers, ~`training data`,     ~`tokens`,
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-125m", "125M",   768,      12, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-350m", "350M",  1024,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "BabyLM", "opt-babylm-1.3B", "1.3B",  2048,      24, "BabyLM (child-available)", "~3B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-160m",     "160M",   768,      12, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-410m",     "410M",  1024,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B",
  "Pythia", "pythia-1.4b",     "1.4B",  2048,      24, "the Pile",                 "~300B") |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrlr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9) |>
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, latex_hline = "major")
```

The six models are listed in @tbl-models. The two families are matched on width rather than on parameter count, which is what the measure is sensitive to: the chance level for overlap is the class subspace rank over the width (Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-math}), so a comparison across models of different width has to be read against different chance levels. Pairing at 768, 1024, and 2048 removes that from the family comparison.

They differ in two ways that matter elsewhere in the paper. The training corpora differ by more than two orders of magnitude in size, which is the manipulation of interest. And they position tokens differently: Pythia uses rotary embeddings, applied inside attention, while OPT learns absolute position embeddings added at the input. Appendix \ref{sec-appendix-positions} uses that difference to rule out absolute position as the source of the interaction.

tibble::tribble(

  "part of speech (noun / verb)",          max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "POS (noun/verb)"]),
  "grammatical role (subject / object)",   max(llm$n_items[llm$construction == "role (subject/object)"])) |>
  mutate(`median tokens` = c(stimmed("pos_noun_verb_form"),
                             stimmed("role_nsubj_obj"))) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrl", linesep = "", escape = FALSE) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 8)

# Standardizing the Hidden States {#sec-appendix-standardize}

Transformer hidden states carry a few dimensions whose variance exceeds the rest by two to three orders of magnitude [@timkey2021bark], and we divide each dimension by its standard deviation before decomposing. The correction is there for the second measure rather than the first. A share is a ratio of squared lengths, and a diagonal rescaling scales the three components alike unless one of them loads disproportionately on the large dimensions, so the sizes are largely unaffected by it. An overlap is a projection onto a subspace estimated from the scatter, and the leading directions of that scatter are set by the largest dimensions, so without the correction every subspace tilts toward the same few axes and unrelated components appear to share directions. The random-subspace baseline does not absorb this, since a random subspace of matched rank is isotropic and inherits none of the tilt, leaving the ratio to chance inflated along with the overlap.

Table \ref{tbl-standardize} reports both readings for part of speech, which was measured twice. The interaction's share is unchanged to three decimals in every model. What moves is the overlaps, and they move in one family: item-class overlap is three to four times larger unstandardized in Pythia and identical to two decimals in OPT-BabyLM. That split is what a rogue-dimension account predicts, since massive activations are documented in the former and the latter is trained on a hundredth of the data; an account on which the correction removes class signal would have to explain why it removes none of it from three of the six models.

The one quantity we would not defend either way is Pythia's class effect, whose share falls by 12 to 31% under the correction. Nothing in the paper turns on its absolute size, and the comparative claim that the interaction runs above it holds under both readings. Grammatical role was measured once, standardized, so the comparison here is for part of speech only.

We use a per-dimension rescaling rather than whitening or a principal-components truncation. Whitening needs the full covariance, which at 768 to 2048 dimensions and roughly 3,700 tokens per grid is near-singular, and making the total scatter isotropic would flatten the between-cell structure the decomposition exists to partition. A truncation discards directions irreversibly and needs a cutoff chosen by hand, and with two classes the class effect spans a single direction that such a cutoff could remove outright. Rotating to principal axes without rescaling changes nothing at all: the decomposition and every quantity we report from it are invariant under orthogonal transformation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-standardize
#| tbl-cap: "Part of speech at the deepest layer, measured with and without the per-dimension rescaling. Sizes are shares of the item-by-class structure; overlaps are the raw fractions, not multiples of chance."
rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |> filter(init == "pretrained") |>
  group_by(model) |> filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup() |>
  left_join(MODELS, by = "model") |> arrange(family, scale) |>
  transmute(model = paste(family, size),
            si = g(std_size_interaction, 3), ri = g(raw_size_interaction, 3),
            sc = g(std_size_class, 3), rc = g(raw_size_class, 3),
            so = g(std_leak_item_into_class, 4), ro = g(raw_leak_item_into_class, 4)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrrrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("model", "std", "raw", "std", "raw", "std", "raw")) |>
  add_header_above(c(" " = 1, "interaction" = 2, "class effect" = 2,
                     "item-class overlap" = 2)) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7)
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Deepest-Layer Measurements {#sec-appendix-llm}

Table \ref{tbl-llm} gives the deepest-layer values behind the curves of @fig-llm, together with the null each overlap is read against.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm
#| tbl-cap: "Deepest-layer measurements, one row per model. The two overlaps are the fraction of the item effect lying in the class subspace and the fraction of the interaction lying in the span of the two main effects, each followed in parentheses by how many times its own rotation null's median it is. That null holds the effect fixed and rotates the target subspace at random 200 times. The class effect and the interaction are shares of the item-by-class structure, with each model's re-split 95% interval in brackets."
llm |> group_by(construction, model) |>
  filter(layer == max(layer)) |> ungroup() |>
  arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
  # One row per model. A median across the six hid exactly what the six are being compared for,
  # and the sizes' re-split intervals are far narrower than the spread across models, so pooling
  # them reported a precision that belonged to a single measurement rather than to the set.
  # Each overlap is against its own model's null rather than r/d: the two differ, since r/d
  # assumes the subspace has its algebraic maximum rank while the projection uses the rank
  # actually fitted, roughly half of it for the marginal subspace.
  transmute(class = shortname(construction),
            model = paste(family, size),
            `item-class overlap` = ov1(leak, leak_null_med, 4),
            `interaction overlap` = ov1(leak_int, leak_int_null_med, 3),
            `class effect` = ci(size_class, size_class_lo, size_class_hi),
            `interaction` = ci(size_int, size_int_lo, size_int_hi)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

## How much of a token the components account for {#sec-appendix-gain}

A share of the item-by-class structure answers how that structure divides. It does not answer how much of a word's representation the structure is, and the two differ by about a factor of three, because most of what varies in a token's hidden state is the context it appears in rather than anything about its word or its class.

Table \ref{tbl-gain} puts the three components in one currency. Take a single token, *walk* used as a noun in some sentence, and ask how well its hidden state can be guessed. Guessing the grand mean is the baseline. Knowing that the word is *walk* removes the *word* column's share of the squared error; knowing further that it is a noun removes the *class effect* column's share; knowing what is specific to *walk*-as-a-noun removes the *interaction* column's. The three components are orthogonal by construction, so each contributes its own term and the columns accumulate.

Two things follow. The class effect, the abstract category the representation is usually said to encode, accounts for `r gr("gb")` of a token; the interaction accounts for `r gr("gg")`, matching or exceeding it in `r gbeat()` of the twelve grids. And nothing here exceeds `r gr("gabg", digits = 0)` at the top end, because the remainder is within-cell context variation, which no item-by-class decomposition sets out to capture.

The last column states the interaction's contribution the other way round, as a share of what the additive account leaves unexplained rather than of the whole. That is the quantity the additive account is judged on, and it runs `r gr("gi")`.

Read geometrically the same quantity looks smaller than it is. The displacement of a cell mean from where an additive account puts it is only about a fifth to a third of the radius of the token cloud around that mean, which invites the reading that the interaction lands inside the cloud and so cannot matter. In 768 to 2048 dimensions that reading does not hold: a cloud is a thin shell with essentially no tokens near its centre, so the observed cell mean fails the same test. Along the direction that actually separates the two classes of a word, the probes of Experiment 3 imply a standardized separation of roughly two to three.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gain
#| tbl-cap: "How much of a token's hidden state each component accounts for, at the deepest layer, as the percentage reduction in squared error against guessing the grand mean. The three components are orthogonal, so their contributions add: *word* plus *class effect* is the additive account, and adding *interaction* gives the full decomposition. *Over additive* restates the interaction the other way round, as a percentage of the error the additive account leaves."
llm_gain |>
  arrange(construction, family, scale) |>
  transmute(class = shortname(construction), model = paste(family, size),
            word = g(100 * ga, 1), cls = g(100 * gb, 1),
            int = g(100 * gg, 1), over = g(100 * gi, 1)) |>
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrrr", linesep = "", escape = TRUE,
      col.names = c("class", "model", "word", "class effect", "interaction",
                    "over additive")) |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("HOLD_position"), font_size = 7) |>
  collapse_rows(1, latex_hline = "major", valign = "top")
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Positional Embeddings Are Not the Source {#sec-appendix-positions}

One architectural explanation of the interaction has to be ruled out before it can be read as a fact about lexical representations. The BabyLMs add a *learned absolute position embedding* at the input. The two classes of a linguistic category are not positionally interchangeable in a sentence, since subjects precede objects and nouns and verbs occupy different slots, so a representation that varies with position varies with the class. If that is what the decomposition is picking up, the interaction would be an artifact of where words sit rather than of how they are represented.

We re-extracted every OPT-BabyLM model with the positional embeddings zeroed out and measured it identically. The ablation was verified per model rather than assumed: with the embedding zeroed, the same token at two different offsets must give identical layer-0 states, and it does, in every model (drift $0.0$ to machine precision). Pythia has no such module, so there is nothing to zero there.

We measure the class effect's share of class-relevant structure which is the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction, which we call the *portable fraction*. If positions were manufacturing the interaction, removing them should leave a larger share of what distinguishes the two classes in a direction shared across words. Absolute sizes cannot be compared here: zeroing the embeddings in a model that was trained with them is a heavy intervention, and it shrinks every component at once, the class effect included.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-posabl
#| tbl-cap: "Trained OPT-BabyLM at the deepest layer, with absolute position embeddings intact and zeroed. Sizes are shares of the item-by-class structure and the portable fraction is the class effect divided by the sum of the class effect and the interaction."
# Read from the main POS file. It carries the *_noposemb inits for every OPT-BabyLM
# size under the current estimator, so this table is on the same footing as every
# other table in the paper. (An older, separate ablation CSV used to hold these rows
# but was written by a superseded measure.py; it has been removed.)
rd("llm_unified_form.csv") |>
  filter(grepl("babylm", model), grepl("^pretrained", init)) |>
  group_by(model, init) |>
  slice_max(layer, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(model = sub(".*/", "", sub("-20eps-seed964", "", model)),
            positions = ifelse(grepl("noposemb$", init), "zeroed", "intact"),
            class = std_size_class, interaction = std_size_interaction,
            portable = std_size_class / (std_size_class + std_size_interaction)) |>
  arrange(match(model, c("opt-babylm-125m", "opt-babylm-350m", "opt-babylm-1.3B")),
          desc(positions)) |>
  transmute(model, positions, `class` = g(class, 3), `interaction` = g(interaction, 3),
            `portable fraction` = g(portable, 3)) |>
  kbl(longtable = FALSE, booktabs = TRUE, align = "llrrr", linesep = "") |>
  kable_styling(font_size = 9)
```

Removing the position embeddings makes these representations *less* separable, not more. The portable fraction falls in every model, from `r pf("125m", "intact")` to `r pf("125m", "zeroed")`, from `r pf("350m", "intact")` to `r pf("350m", "zeroed")`, and from `r pf("1.3B", "intact")` to `r pf("1.3B", "zeroed")` (Table \ref{tbl-posabl}). Whatever the absolute position embedding contributes, it is contributing to the part of class structure that *is* carried by a shared direction. Take it away and what remains is more word-specific, not less. The interaction is not an artifact of position.
